Issued at 310 AM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

Early this morning GOES water vapor imagery and GFS 500mb model 
height analysis showed an upper level low over northern Quebec which 
had retrograded westwards from Newfoundland over the last 24 hours. 
Shortwaves continued to rotate around this low while another 
shortwave originating in Alberta was moving through southern MN. The 
better forcing with this shortwave was remaining further south and 
west of the area so far, keeping the area dry with high level clouds 
overspreading the U.P. The delay in mid-level cloudiness along with 
light winds was helping temperatures cool into the upper 20s and 30s 
away from the lakeshore. Isolated areas of dense fog had formed but 
this should diminish towards sunrise as cloud cover thickens and 
temperatures begin to rise.

The main challenge with the forecast through the end of the week will 
be a favorable setup for lake effect snow as north-northeast flow 
develops over the region and cold air advection increases. 

The upper level low over northern Quebec will continue to move 
southwest to near Lake Huron through Friday with multiple shortwaves 
rotating around the low over the Upper Great Lakes. Scattered rain 
showers, mainly over the southern U.P. are still possible (50% 
chance) through mid-morning but thereafter a cold front will push 
south across the area as the next shortwave drops south out of 
Ontario. Expect temperatures (40s) to slowly fall this afternoon 
over the northern U.P. and lake effect rain showers to become 
widespread as 850mb temperatures fall to -3 to -5C bringing 
sufficient lake-850mb deltaTs (greater than 13C).

The greatest impact period starts late this evening as low levels 
continue to cool bringing 850mb temps down to -6 to -8C and sfc 
temperatures fall to around freezing over the western and central 
U.P., away from the Lake Superior shoreline. The main challenges 
with this forecast is temperatures, snow ratios, snow intensity and 
accumulations. There is enough confidence to issue a Winter Weather 
Advisory as snowfall of 4-8" looks likely (80% chance) over the 
higher terrain of Marquette and Baraga counties, with the high end 
of the range in the higher terrain along and west of the Dead River 
Basin. While this is still on the lower end of traditional
criteria for a 48 hour span, the wet snow character and 
expected moderate rates (0.5-1.0"/hr) support an advisory. Near 
the Lake Superior shoreline less than an inch of accumulation is
expected (Including the city of Marquette); the best chance to 
see any accumulations there would be Thursday night when the 
850mb temps fall to near - 11C. Impacts to the area roads will 
be greatest during the overnight hours tonight and Thursday 
night but periods of heavier snow during the daylight hours will
still be impactful. 

For temperatures the NBM is running much too cold for overnight 
temperatures as it has been trained on recent stretches of cool, 
clear nights. Thus it has temperatures falling into the mid 20s over 
the interior and even below freezing at the immediate lakeshore 
tonight and Thursday night. This seems unlikely given the strong 
onshore flow, cloud cover, precip and marginally cold 850mb temps of 
-6 to -10C. Overall thinking is that temperatures will remain in the 
mid 30s overnight near the Lake Superior shoreline and much of the 
eastern U.P. tonight with slightly cooler temperatures Thursday 
night with the eastern U.P. falling to right around freezing. 

SLRs also look quite a bit overdone in the NBM with 14:1 by Thursday 
including over the Great Lakes. This is seems unlikely given the 
warmer low levels and warm ground temperatures (mid 40s) going into 
the event. Similar thermal profiles to last week's lake effect 
snowfall yielded between 5:1 and 7:1 SLR. These values seem 
reasonable for tonight into Thursday, then approaching 10:1 Thursday 
night as cooling continues. A locally developed temperatures to SLR 
curve matches up well with this for areas away from the lake with 
very low SLRs. RRFS and HRRR also give confidence to the lower SLRs 
as they are producing lower end SLRs, ~6:1 during the daytime hours 
and ~10:1 at night.

While confidence is high in achieving a low end advisory scenario, 
confidence is low with regards to higher end scenarios. While the 
medium range models are producing around 0.5-0.75" QPF over the 
higher terrain the RRFS, HRRR and RAP are much more aggressive with 
1.5 to 2.25" QPF over the high terrain of Marquette and Baraga 
counties. Even with lower end SLRs this would yield warning criteria 
snowfall of 12-16" or more. REFS probabilities for 12"+ over the 
advisory period are in the 30-40% range for the highest terrain. 
Models are converging on a solution of deeper low level moisture 
with inversion heights to 8-10 kft along with strong convergence 
over the east-central part of Lake Superior, into the Marquette
